stories.headline: Haaland's historic goals for Man City in Champions League win at Porto prove his necessity
stories.summary: Erling Haaland scored twice for Man City in their opening win of the Champions League, and it's clear they'd be in trouble without him.
stories.body:
PORTO, Portugal -- Manchester City can always rely on Erling Haaland ... until they can't, and that's when Enzo Maresca will really have to earn his money as Pep Guardiola's successor as manager.

Haaland, the goalscoring phenomenon who carried Norway to the quarterfinals of the World Cup this summer, delivered yet again for Man City by scoring both goals in their 2-0 win against FC Porto in Portugal to kick off their Champions League campaign.

Every time he adds his name to the scoresheet, Haaland seems to create a new record or a piece of club history and in Estadio do Dragao on Tuesday, the 26-year-old moved into third place in City's all-time scoring charts. With 167 goals, he is still 93 behind Sergio Aguero at the top of the list but level with the former Argentina forward as the club's leading scorer in Champions League competition at 36 goals.

Having also scored in this competition for FC Salzburg and Borussia Dortmund, Haaland took his overall Champions League tally to 59, moving him ahead of Thomas Müller into seventh spot in the competition's all-time scorer list.

That's what Haaland does. He has now scored 304 goals in 390 club games since starting out as a 16-year-old with Norwegian team Bryne. His two goals against Porto mean he now has five in five games in all competitions for City this season.

But there is an overriding sense with this City team that once Haaland's goals stop -- either through a loss of form or unavailability -- it will leave a hole that Maresca cannot fill.

It would be stretching it too far to suggest that Haaland is City's greatest strength and potentially their biggest weakness -- goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma might just lay claim to the weakness tag -- but Maresca doesn't have a reliable option to play at centre-forward even if he just wanted to give Haaland a rest.

And that is the problem. While Haaland is fit and scoring, City can challenge for every competition and beat any opponent.

But without him, it would be a different story-- and unless he has the powers of fitness that only Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo have seemed to possess over the last 20 years, then Haaland will have to miss games.

Since he arrived at City from Dortmund ahead of the 2022-23 season, Haaland has only missed 23 games in four seasons, but he is one of the busiest footballers on the planet. With all the competitions he teams qualify for, he has perform in them all until the latter stages -- since the start of the Club World Cup in June 2025, he has played 73 games for club and country.

Does something have to give? Maybe, maybe not, but City are walking on a tightrope with Haaland because of their lack of cover.

Omar Marmoush's loan move to Tottenham last month saw City's designated back-up for Haaland leave the club, so that leaves Maresca with having to deploy wingers such as Antoine Semenyo and Iliman Ndiaye or attacking midfielder Phil Foden in a central role.

They are all good players, and nobody could realistically be a like-for-like replacement for Haalanbd, but they are not centre-forwards.

Arsenal have Kai Havertz and Viktor Gyökeres, Liverpool can use Cody Gakpo as a centre-forward if Alexander Isak is unavailable, while Chelsea signed Danny Welbeck this summer as cover for João Pedro.

Even Manchester United, City's opponents in the Manchester derby at Old Trafford on Sunday, have the options of Bryan Mbeumo, Marcus Rashford or Matheus Cunha if Michael Carrick needs to play without Benjamin Sesko up-front.

Haaland is quite clearly irreplaceable, but it is unusually careless of City not to have at least one player in their squad who is a recognised centre-forward, even as nothing more than an insurance policy.

But against Porto, they didn't need the fallback option because Haaland scored twice in the second-half -- his first a header and the second a calm stoppage time tap-in.

So thanks to Haaland, there was no danger of Donnarumma's nervousness in goal proving costly in terms of the result. The former AC Milan and Paris Saint-Germain goalkeeper, Italy's No. 1, has had a shaky start to the season and has looked uncomfortable with the ball at his feet and when dealing with corners.

He almost conceded an embarrassing goal against Coventry at the weekend, when he allowed the ball to run under his foot before racing back to clear off the line, and there as another worrying moment when an attempted clearance hit Porto winger William Gomes and the ball bounced narrowly wide of the goal.

For a keeper with such a lofty reputation, Donnarumma threatens to be a liability if he continues to perform so erratically, but while Haaland is doing the business at the other end, the 27-year-old is getting away with it.

But if he makes a mistake in a game when Haaland doesn't score, the focus will shift more sharply onto Donnarumma.

Right now, City's season is being defined by Haaland's goals. They won't want it to end up being defined by Donnarumma's mistakes.

stories.headline: Lakers to unveil statue of Hall of Fame coach Phil Jackson
stories.summary: The Lakers are honoring legendary coach Phil Jackson with a statue to be unveiled outside Crypto.com Arena on April 9.
stories.body:
The Los Angeles Lakers will honor Phil Jackson -- who won five of his unprecedented 11 NBA coaching titles in L.A. -- with a statue next season, the team announced Tuesday.

"Phil Jackson defines championship basketball for a reason," Lakers acting governor Jeanie Buss said in a statement. "His masterful approach to coaching brought out the best in some of the greatest athletes to ever play the game. After he accepted my dad's invitation to join the Lakers, Phil's unmatched creativity and commitment to excellence restored our championship legacy, bringing five titles and setting a standard of excellence for generations to come.

"It is a great joy to be able to mark that achievement with the statue he so richly deserves."

The statue will be unveiled April 9, 2027, before the Lakers' game against the Minnesota Timberwolves.

Jackson, 80, coached the Lakers for 11 seasons across two stints (1999-2004, 2005-11), winning three championships running his patented triangle offense through Kobe Bryant and Shaquille O'Neal as the team's primary stars and two more with Bryant and Pau Gasol as L.A.'s lynchpins.

Jackson guided the Lakers to titles in five of seven trips to the NBA Finals, winning in three-peat fashion from 2000-02 and adding back-to-back rings in 2009 and 2010.

Jackson was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2007 and was named as one of the 15 greatest coaches in NBA history when the league revealed its coaching selections as part of its 75th anniversary season.

Jackson will be the ninth member of the Lakers with a statue at Star Plaza outside Crypto.com Arena, joining Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Elgin Baylor, Chick Hearn, Magic Johnson, Pat Riley, Jerry West, O'Neal and Bryant (who has two).

The statue was commissioned by the Lakers to be designed and created by Omri Amrany of Rotblatt Amrany Studio.

stories.headline: Why Bucs' Mayfield has 'extra motivation' heading into season
stories.summary: The self-imposed deadline has passed for Tampa Bay's quarterback as he now turns his attention to the season.
stories.body:
Note: Baker Mayfield and the Bucs agreed to a three-year extension on Monday.

TAMPA, Fla. -- When it comes to playing with a chip on his shoulder and betting on himself, Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield isn't kidding when he says, "That's something I'm pretty familiar with."

Throughout his career, Mayfield has shown both a willingness to fight and prove doubters wrong, but also that his tolerance for what he perceives as disrespect does have its limits. Are the Bucs testing them by having him play out the final year of his deal? Or will they get the most out of a player who "wants his lick back" in 2026?

He didn't get the contract extension he wanted by his self-imposed training camp deadline this summer, and sources say there haven't been any talks since the Bucs' last offer on July 30.

Mayfield said once his deadline expired that he didn't want to have further discussions until the offseason, and he told his agent, Tom Mills, not to bother him unless he's "actually recognized" for his value.

The Bucs have been vocal about not wanting Mayfield to leave, with general manager Jason Licht saying last week during a preseason game broadcast, "I'm very optimistic about it."

"He wants to play," Licht said. "He wants to prove to us that he is the franchise quarterback that we said that he was.

"So, we'll just have to see how it plays out. I'll never close the door on anything in the short term, but right now, he's focused on football."

And then perhaps revealing the volatile nature of these situations, Licht gave a more measured response four days later.

"Well, we certainly respect him wanting to focus on the season," Licht said. "We're focused on the season. I've been here long enough [over 12 years] to know that in this league, I don't want to make predictions on what could happen, what will happen, what won't happen."

Despite the distractions that might come with all of this, Mayfield's teammates have had his back.

"I expect Baker to be Baker, and I expect him to lead us like he always does and I expect him to bring the best out of us," left tackle Tristan Wirfs said. "I think he's gonna play with his hair on fire."

STRAIGHT FROM LUBBOCK, Texas -- following Texas Tech's 41-16 season finale loss to Texas in 2013 -- Mayfield drove his Chevy Tahoe to Austin, right up to the back door of his Lake Travis High School football coach Hank Carter's home for a surprise visit.

Moments before, Carter had been on the phone with a coaching pal at Texas Tech -- where Mayfield had become the first true freshman walk-on quarterback to start a season opener for a BCS school -- and told him, "Hey man, y'all are screwing this up. Why hasn't he been put on scholarship yet?"

Speaking to ESPN, Carter recounted the moment when Mayfield took a seat in his office at his home that day. Not only had Mayfield started seven games for the Red Raiders and accounted for 15 touchdowns and not been put on scholarship, but he was informed that they did not have one available for him that spring and couldn't give him one until something opened up.

And he was informed that coach Kliff Kingsbury was opening up the quarterback job for competition, which didn't sit well.

Carter asked, "Well, what do you think you're going to do?"

Carter said Mayfield responded, "'What am I going to do?' He goes, "I've got all my s--- packed in my car right now. I'm out. I already left."

Carter's response? "Oh my god."

Mayfield delivered the news to Kingsbury on Dec. 10. The following day, when it was announced that he'd won the Big 12 Freshman Offensive Player of the Year award, he made his departure public.

Mayfield and Carter picked up the conversation a few days later. Carter offered to help him find another school. But Mayfield had already made up his mind.

"I think I'm going to go to [Oklahoma]," Mayfield said.

He publicly declared his intentions to enroll there on Dec. 19, and on Jan. 3, the Sooners defeated Alabama 45-31 in the Sugar Bowl, with freshman Trevor Knight at quarterback.

"I go, 'Bake, this quarterback just hung 40 points on Nick Saban,"' Carter said. "I was like, 'Are you sure?'"

Mayfield told him, "Coach, I know that guy. He's a great guy," Carter said. "But then he said, 'I'll beat him out. I'll beat him out. I've wanted to go there my whole life. That's always been the school we rooted for.'

"He was just like, 'Screw it, I'm going,'" Carter said. "And I did not think that was the best decision, but I was wrong. He obviously knew exactly what he was doing. ... And yeah, the rest is history."

A Heisman Trophy, first-overall selection in the 2018 draft and three playoff appearances later, Mayfield finds himself in a situation to prove himself once again with the Bucs, who did not meet his July 28 deadline for a new contract. Instead, he'll play out the remainder of his contract, which ends after the season, and let the chips fall where they may in the offseason.

According to Mayfield, "Sometimes you have to put yourself backed into a corner and fight your way out."

And that's where he stands heading into the season with the Bucs, hoping to lead Tampa back into the playoffs after falling short last year.

"His mentality is that underdog mentality he's had since I'm sure he was 8 years old starting to play football," Tampa Bay offensive coordinator Zac Robinson said. "That'll never leave that guy, and it's a good thing.

"He believes in himself. Whether other people believe in him too, he really doesn't care."

MAYFIELD ASSEMBLED THE team before the Bucs' first camp practice and briefed them on his contract situation, emphasizing that it would not be a distraction and his focus was strictly on them and football. His teammates said the message was heartfelt and well-received.

"I'd say just how committed he is," right guard Cody Mauch said. "I mean, he set a deadline. He said his deadline's the beginning of training camp and he's sticking to it. And now he's like, 'I promise I'm all about ball.'

"It sucks to see him go through this and whatnot, but it's not going to change his mentality, the way he plays. I mean, he's going to go ball out and it's going to get made right."

Wide receiver Tez Johnson said Mayfield has been "true to his word" and "we trust him and we love him."

"When he said it's all ball for us, it was strictly all ball," Johnson said. "He's so eager to just go out there and just prove to the world that he belongs, and he deserves to be in that talk with the quarterbacks."

Nose tackle Vita Vea who had his own contract dispute that was ultimately resolved with a new deal on Aug. 19, empathized with Mayfield's frustration. While Vea was holding in -- attending practices but not participating -- Mayfield used his media availability to not only express frustrations about his own deal but to advocate for Vea's re-signing.

"Baker is the heart and soul of this team," Vea said. "You see the energy he brings on game day. We feed off of that too, not only the offense.

"I hope things get figured out with him. I know we'd all love to have him. Everybody loves Baker. That's somebody that you wish to have on your side on game day."

Mayfield spent the summer working to master Robinson's offense -- his fourth in four seasons in Tampa, although it has strong similarities to the one he operated under Liam Coen in 2024. He's also worked on some of the issues he felt he fell short in last year, like his rhythm and needing to tighten up his footwork.

"If you're out of rhythm in this system -- whether it's timing of the routes and the concepts -- bad things are going to happen," Mayfield said. "It starts with my feet and going through that and trusting the timing of that and going through the progressions, checking the ball down."

Quarterbacks coach Chandler Whitmer, who spent last season tutoring Heisman Trophy winner Fernando Mendoza en route to a national championship at Indiana, has been a stickler for footwork, to the point that Mayfield has joked that he wants to "put his little ass in a headlock and beat him up."

Mayfield then conceded, "But no, I like to be coached hard."

Licht, who has been on the opposite side of the table during those difficult contract talks, is seeing him demand even more of himself and believes he could possibly have the best year of his career.

"Shoot, he gets in here at probably 4 a.m," Licht said. "I can just see it. Not that he wasn't before, but I just see a bit extra motivation on his part."

LAST SEASON WAS an injury-marred season -- not just for Mayfield, but for almost his entire cast of receivers, starting offensive line and running back Bucky Irving.

As a result, Mayfield wasn't as physically effective after an MVP-caliber start, but he scoffed at the notion that the team's hesitancy at a deal longer than two years stems from concern about his body holding up.

"I started every game last year ... the last three years," Mayfield said. "I don't know if that should ever be a question."

Mayfield's combined 51 starts over the last three years ties him with Jared Goff of the Detroit Lions and Josh Allen of the Buffalo Bills for the most quarterback starts in the regular season in that span. But he's taken 116 sacks (fourth most) in that span and been contacted 345 times (12th most).

"I think he's very mindful of that," Licht said. "I think all quarterbacks, as they progress through their career, I think they are a little bit more in tune with that."

Mayfield did admit on the "4th and South" podcast that he's intentionally taken hard hits to light a spark when making plays outside the pocket.

"Sometimes it might be first down, but our team's in a lull," Mayfield said. "There's certainly points I can definitely be better about it, and I know that. But every once in a while, the guys need a little kick in the ass."

The Glazers, who own the Buccaneers, have never had to sign off on top-dollar quarterback money. They won their first Super Bowl with veteran journeyman Brad Johnson, who was not under a lucrative deal. Even when seven-time Super Bowl winner Tom Brady signed with the Buccaneers, he averaged $25 million per season. Twelve quarterbacks will make at least double that in 2026.

In their initial talks, Mayfield said the Bucs were "not anywhere close" to what he and his agent were looking for -- not to reset the market but to be in the range of his peers. Sources told ESPN's Jeremy Fowler that Mayfield and his agent used Green Bay's Jordan Love (four years, $55 million per year, $160.3 million total guaranteed), Jacksonville's Trevor Lawrence (five years, $55 million per year, $200 million total guaranteed), and San Francisco's Brock Purdy (five years, $53 million per year, $182.55 million total guaranteed) as comps during the negotiations.

Fowler also reported that in the Bucs' last offer prior to camp, they did come in offering a two-year deal worth slightly above $100 million in total. But Mayfield wanted longer than that and he was dissatisfied with the guaranteed money.

Per a source with knowledge of the situation, Mayfield's issue wasn't just length of the deal or guaranteed money. While he did not set out to reset the market, $50 million per year would have put Mayfield 13th in the league among current deals.

But those numbers will jump significantly over the next eight to 12 months because several quarterbacks are in line or eligible for new deals in Lamar Jackson, C.J. Stroud, Caleb Williams, Drake Maye, Bo Nix and Jayden Daniels. The $50 million benchmark today will be $60 million soon, a source explained. Another not involved in Mayfield's negotiations but who represents one of those quarterbacks believes there will indeed be at least one $70 million quarterback. What also must be considered is that the salary cap is expected to rise.

When asked about ownership's comfort level in spending that kind of money long-term and the thought process in making that type of investment, Licht said, "You're always comfortable with a great player and you make things work."

Mayfield is also having to navigate the loss of his top wideout and the franchise's all-time leading scorer in Mike Evans, whose departure in free agency for the San Francisco 49ers sent shockwaves throughout the team.

Then he spent large portions of camp without three of his top four wide receivers in Jalen McMillan (knee sprain), Emeka Egbuka (toe sprain) and Johnson (groin strain). On top of that, Wirfs missed nearly all of camp with a hamstring strain but he returned to practice.

Wirfs returned to practice Aug. 19 and Johnson Aug. 25. On Wednesday, before the team broke for four days, McMillan and Egbuka were running off to the side with the training staff.

They all should be ready for the season, with Bowles saying "They're headed in the right direction," but Mayfield believes their absences gave them a chance to explore different packages and work on his rapport with rookie third-round draft pick Ted Hurst III, who the Bucs believe possesses a lot of the physical attributes as Evans.

"You can just see it in [Mayfield's] eyes every time he takes the field," Johnson said. "When he's in a huddle calling a play, he's very intentional with the young guys and just getting them to learn because it's a moving train."

Mayfield threw a jump ball to Hurst during a two-minute drill in joint practices at the New York Jets. While he didn't come down with it, Hurst told ESPN it "gave me a sense that he believes in me to attack the ball."

Which is where Mayfield is now, attacking his preparation for Week 1 at the Cincinnati Bengals on Sept. 13 (1 p.m. ET, FOX). He's aware that some prognosticators have expressed doubts about a team without Evans, and about his health, or how a looming contract situation could negatively impact his headspace -- never mind that he embraces the motivation.

"Baker's pissed off every year and every game," Bowles told WDAE radio this week. "He wants to beat the piss out of somebody. This is nothing new. It's a normal deal for him, whether it was a contract or not. We'll get the best Baker Mayfield that you can probably get."

Carter added, "He loves that. I don't think he always did love it. Certainly growing up -- that's not something that feels great, but I think now he's a master at it. And so any type of adversity that comes his way, he's just going to be like, 'Okay, no problem. We're going to figure this out.' And that's what he does well."

Mauch believes Mayfield when he says, "It's only going to get worse from here."

"He's going to go off," Mauch said. "... No doubt in my mind, he's going to go up and [and put up MVP or Offensive Player of the Year numbers] and get even more money now. So it's going to work out better for him in the end. I'm excited to see the way Bake uses this year."

Carter is excited as well, because he knows firsthand what can come of doubting his former player.

"I mean, he's always had the mindset of, 'Yeah, I'm not going to let you get one over on me,' Carter said. "That's kind of his deal. I've been saying this about him for a long time. I believe in trends, so I know how it'll work out for Baker. It's going to work out good because it always does."

stories.headline: Transfer rumors, news: Man City eye move for Atleti's Baena
stories.summary: Manchester City are looking to sign World Cup-winning midfielder Álex Baena from Atlético Madrid. Transfer Talk has the latest.
stories.body:
Manchester City are looking at signing yet another midfielder, while Real Madrid are eyeing up Declan Rice, but Arsenal are making moves to keep him. Join us for the latest transfer news and rumors from around the globe.

Transfers home page | Men's summer grades | Women's grades

Trending rumors

- Manchester City are looking at Atlético Madrid midfielder Álex Baena, Football Insider reports. It is said that the Citizens are admirers of the 25-year-old, who is being considered for a future transfer as an option to reinforce the left flank, though any deal is unlikely to be pursued in January unless reinforcements are needed. Baena started seven games for Spain at the World Cup, and he is also on the radar of Newcastle United and Aston Villa.

- Real Madrid are interested in Arsenal midfielder Declan Rice, TEAMtalk reports. The club's hierarchy are reportedly keen on the 27-year-old and pushing to make him a priority signing, but manager Mikel Arteta is keen to keep his title-winning side together. Transfer journalist Nicolo Schira reports that the Gunners are already preparing contract talks with Rice amid plans to offer him a deal that will secure his future at the club until the summer of 2031. He has previously rejected interest from clubs in the Saudi Pro League.

- Arsenal hold interest in Al Ahli striker Ivan Toney, according to TEAMtalk. The Gunners are reported to be exploring the market to find a potential replacement for Viktor Gyökeres should he leave the Emirates Stadium, and they see Toney, 30, as a player who could come in as a back-up option behind starter Kai Havertz. An impressive start to the Saudi Pro League campaign has seen Toney score six goals in five matches.

- Manchester United aren't considering a move for free agent defender David Alaba despite reports, according to Manchester Evening News. The Premier League side are said to have ruled out an approach for the 34-year-old, with plans to focus their transfer strategy on acquiring young players with significant potential. Alaba, who has also been linked with Lazio, made 11 appearances in La Liga for Real Madrid last season. He hasn't played competitively since starring four times for Austria at the World Cup.

- Free agent striker Anthony Martial has received offers from Everton and two clubs in Ligue 1, Foot Mercato reports. The 30-year-old is attracting interest from several clubs following the termination of his deal with Liga MX side Monterrey, but after not being promised a starting role, he has decided against accepting a proposal. Martial's last salary was believed to be in the region of €3.5 million per season.

Other rumors
- Inter Milan were willing to part ways with defender Alessandro Bastoni for €70 million in the summer. (Diario AS)

- Liverpool have been offered the chance to sign free agent right back Dani Carvajal. (TEAMtalk)

- Arsenal and Manchester City are keeping close tabs on Paris Saint-Germain defender Willian Pacho. (Caught Offside)

- Chelsea explored an approach for Fulham midfielder Sander Berge after their move for Monaco's Lamine Camara broke down. (BBC Sport)

- Brentford have opened contract talks with winger Kevin Schade amid interest from Arsenal. (TEAMtalk)

- Chelsea considered a move for free agent midfielder Renato Sanches. (Foot Mercato)

- Palmeiras striker Vitor Roque is attracting interest from Manchester United and Chelsea. (Ekrem Konur)

- Liverpool winger Federico Chiesa will explore an exit from the club in January if he does not play more matches. (Football Insider)

- Free agent winger Jadon Sancho has received an approach from two clubs in the Premier League. He remains on the radar of Borussia Dortmund. (TEAMtalk)

- Liverpool are pleased with the acquisition of on-loan Barcelona defender Ronald Araujo. They have the option to sign him permanently for £47 million. (Diario Sport)

- FC Krasnodar are interested in Flamengo forward Everton Cebolinha. (GE Globo)

- Roma are considering an approach for free agent left back Raphael Guerreiro. (Ekrem Konur)

- Lecce midfielder Omri Gandelman is on the radar of Maccabi Haifa. (Nicolo Schira)

Check out all of our starting pitcher rankings and other lineup selection tools here to help you make smart fantasy baseball lineup decisions. All fantasy advice is geared toward ESPN 10-team leagues with standard scoring.

Pitchers to stream on Wednesday

It's been a mixed bag for Blade Tidwell after entering the San Francisco Giants rotation in early August. He passes the eye test, but his 4.99 ERA and 1.30 WHIP as a starter over 30 2/3 frames indicate he has work to do. Control is his main issue, with improving sequencing and gaining consistency also needed. This recommendation is based on a favorable home matchup with the St. Louis Cardinals, whose wOBA facing right-handers has been in the bottom third of the league all season.
Kade Anderson has yet to deliver on the hype through three major league starts. His fourth is against the Texas Rangers at pitcher-friendly T-Mobile Park. The Rangers continue to sit within striking distance of the AL West title or a wild card berth despite posting the second-lowest wOBA and third-highest strikeout rate facing left-handers over the past month.
Cal Quantrill has quietly emerged as one of the best pitchers in the league down the stretch, as evidenced by his 1.16 ERA and 0.81 WHIP with 30 strikeouts and just five walks over his last 31 frames. Next up is a juicy road date as the Rangers face Anderson and the Seattle Mariners. While they've been better lately, the Mariners still sport one of the lowest wOBAs in the league versus right-handers.
Will Warren figures to bounce between the rotation and bullpen down the stretch. He's been tabbed as Wednesday's starter when the New York Yankees entertain the Colorado Rockies. The Rockies aren't a pushover away from Coors Field, but it's still a favorable matchup as the Yankees try to fend off the Boston Red Sox for the top American League wild card spot.

Hitters to stream on Wednesday

Coby Mayo is crushing left-handers this season, sporting a .323/.384/.752 line facing southpaws. Next up is a date with lefty Foster Griffin when the Baltimore Orioles host the Cleveland Guardians. While he's done a better job keeping the ball in the yard lately, Foster has surrendered 23 homers in 160 1/3 innings, and his strikeout rate has plummeted recently.
Heriberto Hernandez of the Miami Marlins lines up for a productive evening with the New York Mets visiting Little Havana. Robert Stock will take the hill, and even though he holds the platoon edge, Hernandez has handled right-handers competently, clubbing 14 of his 24 homers against righties.
Nolan Arenado has slumped a bit over the second half, but he's still potent against left-handers. The Arizona Diamondbacks are on the road for a series with the Kansas City Royals. Daniel Lynch IV gets the call for the home team, and while he generally keeps the ball in the yard, he's vulnerable to right-handed batters and has fanned only six over his previous 16 2/3 innings, while walking half a dozen batters.
Ty France and the San Diego Padres host Jackson Kent and the Washington Nationals. France has settled in as the everyday first baseman, hitting lefties and righties equally well. Still, it helps to enjoy the platoon advantage, and the left-handed Kent has a 5.55 ERA and 1.68 WHIP over his first five career starts, spanning 24 1/3 stanzas.

stories.headline: Germany beats South Korea, rolls into World Cup quarterfinals
stories.summary: Host Germany advanced to the quarterfinals of the women's FIBA World Cup with a morale-boosting 94-56 rout of South Korea on Tuesday, and the United States learned its next opponent.
stories.body:
BERLIN -- Host Germany advanced to the quarterfinals of the women's FIBA World Cup with a morale-boosting 94-56 rout of South Korea on Tuesday, and the United States learned its next opponent.

Hungary, which beat Japan 84-63, will play the four-time defending champion U.S. on Thursday.

Germany captain Marie Gülich led her team to a quarterfinal against European champion Belgium with 19 points and five rebounds.

Every German score elicited huge cheers from the appreciative home fans at the Berlin Arena, particularly in the first half. Germany led by 17 points at halftime.

The home team has been gradually improving since losing its first group game by 30 points to Spain. Germany rebounded with a 74-58 win over Japan and followed with an 83-58 win over Mali.

Hungary eliminates Japan Réka Lelik led Hungary with 23 points and eight rebounds in a surprisingly comfortable win over Japan earlier.

Virág Takács-Kiss also had eight rebounds and added 17 points for Hungary, which will face the U.S. in the late quarterfinal slot Thursday.

"It feels incredible. It's been 40 years since we went to the quarterfinals and I still can't believe it," Lelik said.

The game was overshadowed by a serious injury to Japan shooting guard Saki Hayashi, who went off with what looked a broken right arm after an awkward fall.

Hayashi needed immediate medical attention a foul in the air from Agnes Torok with just over a minute left in the second quarter. A blue tarp was provided to give her privacy and fans responded with applause when she was led off.

Japan connected on only seven 3-pointers Tuesday. The Japanese had set a record with 20 three-pointers in a World Cup game on Friday before France broke it with 22 on Monday.

Ramu Tokashiki's two free throws drew Japan level at 34-34, but that was as close as it got. Agnes Studer responded with a 3-pointer to give Hungary a 37-34 lead at halftime.

"They hit their open shots, we missed our open shots," Japan coach Corey Gaines said.

Hungary finished 11 of 25 from beyond the arc on the first of two days off for the U.S., which qualified directly for the quarterfinals as a group winner.

"I'm excited to play the very best players in the world, the best team in the word," Lelik said of Thursday's game. "I never got the opportunity to play against them. So I'm just very excited how it's going to be. And we're going to do everything for sure. But besides that, I want us to enjoy the game."

Still two places up for grabs All the quarterfinals are scheduled for Thursday. Spain and France await the winners of Wednesday's playoffs between Italy-Australia and China-Puerto Rico, respectively.

stories.headline: Under pressure: those with the biggest questions to answer in the semis
stories.summary: Two cut-throat AFL semifinals. Two of four teams facing the end of the road. And that means a host of individuals, players and coaches are under pressure. Rohan Connolly looks at who has the biggest questions to answer.
stories.body:
Two cut-throat AFL semifinals. Two of four teams facing the end of the road. That's the equation. And that means a host of individuals, players, and coaches are ... under pressure (yep, that Queen/David Bowie classic's going through my head now, too).

Go on, put it on and click your fingers to that bassline while you read about those most under the pump on Friday and Saturday evening.

Justin Longmuir
You won't find too many better recent examples of one result so starkly changing the narrative surrounding an AFL coach than Fremantle's loss to Hawthorn last Thursday night. Longmuir and his team had done everything right this season until then. Yet the bottom line remains they now teeter on the edge of a straight sets exit at home with Longmuir copping plenty of critical flak. The Dockers' ball movement was stymied, they were inefficient, with 57 forward entries producing only five goals, and Hawthorn created space far too easily. The "lack of flexibility" accusation has also popped up again, along with more talk about costly poor starts. Fremantle lost a home final last year to Gold Coast. A third home finals defeat in a row could damage Longmuir's reputational stocks irreparably.

Jeremy Cameron
There may not be another player under as much pressure to perform on Friday night as the dual Coleman medallist, who has been goalless for a month, and five times in his last seven outings. Cameron took just one mark and had only nine disposals against Carlton last week, lacked any sort of physical presence, and was drifting up around the wing to pick up what few touches he could manage. Cameron managed two goals in Geelong's narrow Round 15 loss to Fremantle in Perth, but even then the Cats were held to the second-lowest score of their last 10 outings. Anything less this week, and there will be an awful lot of responsibility upon the likes of Shannon Neale and Patrick Dangerfield to find Cameron's missing goals.

Josh Treacy
What's that expression, one day a rooster the next a feather duster? On August 25, Fremantle's Josh Treacy was being feted as the All-Australian centre half-forward for 2026. Just over a week later, he was getting towelled up by the critics for being "destroyed" by Hawthorn key defender Josh Battle. Treacy had just four disposals, no marks and kicked just one late consolation goal. He hadn't had a kick until late in the last quarter and was accused of not attacking the contest with his usual physical presence. It doesn't get any easier this week for him, either, given that last time Fremantle met Geelong, Connor O'Sullivan held him to 2.2 from only nine disposals, picking up 16 himself, six intercept marks and a coaches' vote. Treacy needs to improve on that effort and last week's significantly.

Patrick Dangerfield
Hang on. How can the best player on the ground in last week's elimination final be under pressure the very next game he plays? Well, being the long-time acknowledged champion he is, the Brownlow medallist is always under the microscope to an extent. If "Danger" plays a blinder, Geelong will generally win. That's pressure of its own. But then there's the memory of last year. Prior to last Friday night, it was in the 2025 preliminary final against Hawthorn that Dangerfield delivered his best September performance with 31 disposals and three goals. And the following week? Unfortunately, his banged-up 35-year-old frame couldn't repeat the dose, delivering a strangely muted 10-disposal effort in the grand final loss to Brisbane. Now, 12 months older, can he back up one superlative September effort with another?

Murphy Reid
Last year's Rising Star and this year's All-Australian might be a bit of a soft target given what he's done in two seasons, that he's only recently turned 20 and last week played only his second AFL final, but Reid was one of the biggest disappointments in Fremantle's soft qualifying final performance. Whether missing the two games prior with a groin niggle has thrown him out of his stride is an interesting question, but his usually precise kicking was unusually off-target against the Hawks, and his off night was a major factor in Fremantle lacking so much of the spark the headbanded youngster has brought to the team and which had typified their season to date.

Lachie Neale
The dual Brownlow medallist was hardly the only Lion to have a poor one last week, but there's several reasons he's probably under more pressure than nearly all his teammates this week. Most obviously, given the widespread expectation that he's headed elsewhere in 2027, this could well be his final game for the club. And after the pantsing Brisbane's engine room copped against the Swans and Neale's blanketing by Jai Serong, there's another massive personal challenge ahead in the shape of Geelong tagger Oisin Mullin, who's shut him down successfully before. Intriguingly, too, Neale has never polled a single Brownlow vote against the Cats. His record in finals overall is stellar, but Brisbane has seldom needed one of his best September performances more.

Matthew Nicks
OK, let's be clear, Nicks isn't going to lose his job if Adelaide can't pull an upset against Brisbane at the Gabba, even though he might have had the Crows not beaten the Bulldogs last week. But pressure? That hasn't suddenly evaporated just because a rested Adelaide beat a lesser-ranked opponent at home and gave Nicks his first finals win. The stigma of last year's straight sets elimination remains strong, the Crows won three fewer games this season and finished five spots lower on the ladder, and their record against the very best in 2026 is hardly inspiring, 2-5 against the top five, including a 52-point thumping at the hands of Saturday's opponent at the same venue. Victory this time would absolutely shore up Nicks' credentials. Another bad loss? The question marks will intensify.

Brisbane's key defenders
Saturday was a horror show for the whole Brisbane line-up, but no-one more than its defenders, and its talls in Harris Andrews, Darcy Gardiner and Ryan Lester specifically, with Sydney pair Charlie Curnow and Logan McDonald booting 11 goals between them. McDonald successfully curbed Andrews' intercepting ability and cashed in with half-a-dozen goals, and Curnow smashed Gardiner. And the equation doesn't get any easier this week with Adelaide's three-pronged tall forward set-up featuring Riley Thilthorpe, Taylor Walker and Darcy Fogarty, who Stats Mate tells us has kicked at least two goals in his last eight games. Ty Gallop surely is a good chance of returning at Gardiner's expense, or even second ruck Darcy Fort. But whatever selection strings coach Chris Fagan pulls, the Lions can't afford their key backs to be anywhere near that bad again.

You can read more of Rohan Connolly's work at FOOTYOLOGY.

stories.headline: George Russell follows Lando Norris in getting Silverstone grandstand
stories.summary: George Russell has got his wish after his grandstand joust with Lando Norris at Silverstone.
stories.body:
George Russell has got his wish after his grandstand joust with Lando Norris at Silverstone.

The Mercedes man has followed in his McLaren rival's footsteps as Silverstone announced the George Russell Grandstand would be opened at the circuit's Farm Curve for next year's race.

Norris debuted his 'Landostand' in 2025 when he claimed his maiden British Grand Prix win and this year 16,000 fans packed it out at Stowe corner.

Russell revealed his desire to also have a grandstand for his own race and quipped during this year's Silverstone weekend that he quite fancied taking some of Norris' seats.

"Good luck," Norris retorted. "I have more passionate fans and a better fanbase I think. Mine was more wanted from a public point of view, which is a great thing.

"He can do what he wants, but he is certainly not taking any of my seats."

stories.headline: How to draft, play and win your fantasy hockey league like an expert
stories.summary: It's not just who you draft, it's everything that happens after. An expert guide to play fantasy hockey like the pros.
stories.body:
Let's go! Coming off a long summer following one of the most exciting hockey seasons ever, on and off the NHL ice, we're ready to re-embrace the game we love, as both fans and invested fantasy managers. Whether you're a wily veteran or brand new to the game, we're here to help you not only compete but give yourself a solid shot at victory. Starting with this primer that serves as an introduction for newbies and a refresher for those more well-versed.

More: Sign up for free | Rankings | Projections | League types

The draft

The most important two hours of your entire fantasy hockey season. But don't sweat it! A little research and preparation is all it takes to cobble together a competitive roster. To start, don't overcomplicate matters, take the best player available. This year, that's Nathan MacKinnon, Nikita Kucherov, Macklin Celebrini, or Connor McDavid (yes, even under new defensive-minded head coach Mike Babcock).

Once that elite quartet is off the board, turn to the second tier of elite forwards including Leon Draisaitl, Jason Robertson, and David Pastrnak. Your blue line and net can wait a moment. Cale Makar isn't fetching you fantasy points for dollars earned and there are enough good-to-great goalies even once Andrei Vasilevskiy is off the table. Grab your big scorer up front, first and foremost. These are the skaters who can average 3.0-plus per game in ESPN standard points leagues.

Use the next few early rounds to acquire at least one premiere fantasy defenseman and a top-tier netminder (more on those positions below), while always keeping an eye out for the remaining gems up front. Don't fret about filling positional requirements at this stage and continue to grab the heavy hitters. I promise the fantasy math will eventually work out in your favor.

Okay, once the best players are off the board, and your top-tier goalie is secured, now start working to satisfy positional and categorical needs. Too many right-wingers will result in too many quality performers stuck on your bench on busier nights. While a dearth at another position is also frustratingly limiting. Of course, if your league adheres to the overarching (F) classification, continue to draft the best player available. In later rounds, it's time to really focus on sleepers, bounce-back and breakout contenders. These potential pleasant surprises can truly alter a roster for the better.

Back to the importance of research and preparation, as usual, we're here to help with preseason previews covering all matters fantasy hockey right up until your draft and beyond.

ESPN Fantasy Hockey is the fun, free way to get inside the game. Draft your players, set your lineups and earn points when the pros do. Sign up today!

Bounce-back and breakout candidates

With the top center in San Jose serving as the poster child for breakout candidates in 2025-26, Celebrini wasn't alone in taking a leap forward. The Anaheim Ducks' Cutter Gauthier impressed us with his 41-goal statement season just as (then) Tampa Bay Lightning defender Darren Raddysh won over alert managers by finishing 11th in fantasy points, despite missing nine games. Cole Caufield followed linemate Nick Suzuki's lead from the previous season by exploding for 88 points, including 51 goals. Will linemate Juraj Slafkovsky be next in busting through the 80-point mark? Meanwhile in Philadelphia, Dan Vladar proved he does indeed have the chops to serve as a No. 1 netminder. Easier said than done, but spotting these characters before they erupt can go a long way to ameliorating your fantasy squad.

Zach Benson of the Buffalo Sabres could be one such candidate, after making such a positive impression this past spring. Poised to see top-line minutes alongside Tage Thompson, the scrappy winger feels on the verge of going next-level. Celebrini's roommate, Will Smith is also in ideal position to erupt at age 21. On the blue line, I like Cole Hutson of the Washington Capitals to wow us as a rookie, and Jet Greaves is in position to finally establish himself as a prominent fantasy netminder for the Columbus Blue Jackets.

As for bounce-back performers, goalie Jeremy Swayman and forward Ryan O'Reilly are just two examples of figures who rebounded off rather drab campaigns the previous year. Now I have my sights set on Tampa Bay's Brayden Point and Capitals newbie Jordan Kyrou to do the same. Elias Pettersson is an intriguing figure -- altogether not a bad fantasy performer despite his disappointing play in Vancouver -- as someone who might finally get back to the player he was under new management and a fresh coaching staff. The former 100-point forward very much might be worth a roll of the fantasy dice.

Less appealing "B" candidates

Backsliders. Maybe they're coming off a season that's just too anomalous and tough to duplicate. Age could be another factor, along with a new role within the lineup or on another team altogether. Whatever the reason, these players are moving in the wrong direction production-wise, and you want to avoid them.

Boston's Morgan Geekie potted 25 goals in his first 36 games and then just another 14 in the following 45 contests. Managers unfamiliar with that timing and trend might be unjustifiably wooed by the total of 39 and mistake the winger for a 40-goal scorer. When in reality, even if he remains on a top line with Pastrnak, the 28-year-old sports true 30-goal potential at heart.

Does Alex DeBrincat score another 40-plus with Patrick Kane back in Chicago? Considering that loss and the state of hockey with the Detroit Red Wings at present, I wouldn't predict as much. Sure, ex-Sabre Alex Tuch could flirt with the 35-goal and 70-point mark once more on a line with Dylan Strome and Alex Ovechkin in Washington, or enjoy more modest numbers on another unit. Just as some players are going to improve statistically with a different supporting cast, others will move in the opposite direction, and expectations should be tempered.

This isn't to suggest you shouldn't draft Geekie, DeBrincat, Tuch and others, just don't jump on them too early with the mind you're getting last year's exact fantasy model.

More on goalies

You won't win your league, or even make a go of it, with bad fantasy goaltending. Snoozing on this position is not an option. These few competitors are responsible for far too many categories. So as tempting as it may be to snag another high-performing skater when it's the right time to address your needs in net, take the latter route.

The first rule of thumb is to avoid netminders on lousy teams. Arguably the best goaltender in the world played 57 games for a surprisingly bad squad in Winnipeg this past season. By the time mid-April rolled around, Connor Hellebuyck netted his managers fewer fantasy points than 27 others in the league. Taking large personal strides, Spencer Knight served as a promising figure for the Blackhawks through yet another rebuilding campaign in Chicago. Yet despite making 22 more starts than Jesper Wallstedt in Minnesota, Knight still finished well below the Wild netminder in the fantasy standings. No matter how individually talented, great goalies on an inferior teams most often aren't in position to regularly reward their managers.

But busy is good too. Once zoned in on the better teams in the league, it's wise to target those who play the most. Tampa Bay's Vasilevskiy is a great example, as is Dallas Stars netminder Jake Oettinger. Logan Thompson presents as a top-five fantasy netminder, again, on a Capitals team that should be even better. While the league continues to trend in the direction of relying on two or more figures between the pipes, there's still a good number of goalies who carry a significantly heavier workload. Such characters on quality squads need to be chased, first and foremost.

After your top performers are secured, give prominent starters on improving teams and top-tier tandem members a look. It's Greaves' net in Columbus. If the Blue Jackets can equal or improve-upon their record from this past run, the 25-year-old will prove valuable. As for old faces in new places, ex-New Jersey Devils netminder Jacob Markstrom could be in for nice rebound campaign with the Florida Panthers.

Colorado's Scott Wedgewood reigns supreme as member of the tandem crowd, while Stanley Cup Champ Brandon Bussi should see more starts than Pyotr Kotchetkov now that Frederik Andersen is in Edmonton. The options open up considerably, again, once your recognized heavy-hitters are in place.

For more on how to address this all-important position, check out our dedicated goalie preview.

A slightly deeper dive on D-men

Unlike in years past, Makar is no longer a list of one as far as premier fantasy defenders are concerned. Six blueliners -- Makar, Zach Werenski, Evan Bouchard, Moritz Seider, Charlie McAvoy and Jake Sanderson -- all averaged between 2.4 and 2.6 fantasy points/game in ESPN standard leagues this past season. While Makar and Bouchard sit a titch above the rest, the gap is much smaller than before. Another good throng, including Quinn Hughes, Rasmus Dahlin and Lane Hutson, banged out 2.2 points/game in 2025-26. In most leagues, you want at least one top-tier performer, along with a pair from that secondary, yet still impressive, sub-set. Then take a breath.

In competition that rewards blocked-shots, there's no real sense of urgency in padding your fantasy roster with defenders. This past campaign, 29 blueliners earned between 1.7 and 2.1 fantasy points/game. Plenty to go around. Instead, pursue skaters that are going to put up the flashiest numbers first, regardless of position. Of course, as with every position, when rounding out your defensive corps, keep an eye out for prospective breakout candidates. The Los Angeles Kings' Brandt Clarke and Capitals rookie Cole Hutson are two such names on my 2026-27 radar.

Leagues, leagues, leagues

As for customization, ESPN Fantasy provides the forum to create any type of league you want. If interested in constructing your own head-to-head competition, first settle on either the points or categories path, then determine the applicable stats. Beyond scoring, hits and blocked-shots -- to reward defensive play -- are more popular than ever. Maybe you're a faceoff enthusiast, and want to compensate the best and busiest in the dot. Have a penchant for penalty minutes? PIM remains an option, along with a good variety of others to suit your fantasy hockey tastes. Managers who don't care to customize can always opt for our default head-to-head points league, referenced above, which remains widely popular.

For those who want to kick it old school, Rotisserie (Roto) competition awards points based on where your players rank as a collective in every category. For instance, in a 12-team league, the group of skaters that boasts the most total goals, at any given time, retain the maximum 12 points. The fantasy team with the worst plus/minus receives just one. And so on, cumulatively and fluidly, through each category to arrive at a combined sum. H2H category leagues differ from points leagues in that not only one goal, but one hit or one blocked-shot, can mean the difference between victory and defeat regarding that particular stat. Scores carry forward and add up throughout the campaign -- say, 6-4, then 3-7 etc. -- unlike in a head-to-head points battle where you either win the week or you don't.

Once the parameters and makeup of your league are set, decide how much time you want to invest in adjusting your lineup. Every day, every week, or never again, in honor of how we used to pen-and-paper-it back in the pre-internet days of yore.

Made it this far? Create your own league with your own rules and play against your friends today.

Categories matter

Becoming intimately acquainted with your league's specific categories is essential to success. Not only with the stats themselves, but how much weight they carry. One hit in category leagues makes a greater impact than when only worth 0.1 points otherwise. If assists are equivalent to goals, Lane Hutson is nearly equal to Makar as a fantasy performer. Conversely, a sniper like Steven Stamkos (at least in his second season with the Nashville Predators) boasts a lot more shine in fantasy competition where goals double helpers in value. If blocked-shots don't count, a defender like Toronto's Jake McCabe belongs nowhere near your fantasy roster. Anyway, you get the idea.

Investing in mock drafts

The more you mock draft, the better. While practice doesn't necessarily make perfect in this case, it certainly helps. These dress rehearsals will offer you insight as to how other managers are navigating the draft along with player preferences. If everyone is avoiding a high-ranked skater there's likely a reason why. You'll also be better prepared for certain trends -- a too-early run on goalies, for instance -- after experiencing one for pretend. Plus, they're fun. Check out our Mock Draft Lobby, pick the room that best represents your own fantasy league, and take a spin.

Not sure how to play? Try out the ESPN Mock Draft Lobby.

Building a dynasty

This style of fantasy competition suits those who want to play the long game. Most akin to the real-life NHL affair, managing a dynasty hockey squad requires patience and foresight. Barring trades, you're stuck with these players, like it or not, for the haul. Last season, I recommended grabbing Matthew Schaefer right off the top, even if he didn't end up playing in the NHL full-time (a laughable concept now). This year, that's Leafs No. 1 pick Gavin McKenna, who is expected to suit up right away. Our fantasy rookie rundown will further help with who to target for what's likely to be a long, and hopefully happy, dynasty fantasy marriage.

Keeper leagues are different in that you're able to jettison your lesser players each season and keep only those most treasured. How to approach the draft in rounding out your roster largely depends on your club's current state. Are you rich with peak talent and ready to win now? Then go on and grab some aging veterans to help with that championship push. Otherwise, if your team is still also in the building phase, similar to many real NHL clubs, it's wiser to invest in younger, gifted players who sport the wherewithal to be great down the road.

Roster maintenance

This is the fun part. Outside of set-and-forget leagues, how well you fiddle with your roster will determine whether you're still in the championship hunt once spring rolls around, or already looking ahead to next season. Striking the right balance is of ultimate importance, as too much tinkering -- for instance losing patience with an underperforming player and prematurely letting them go -- can also bite you in the behind.

Even before puck-drop on day one, it's essential to become familiar with your pool of available free agents. I guarantee a few will emerge as valuable fantasy performers in those first few weeks, or even days. Whether their success is due to an unexpected line assignment or another factor. Trust me, these players will already be rostered by the most vigilant managers before others even realize what's going on. To repeat, the first few weeks of the season are absolutely integral in allowing you the chance to improve your roster, by swapping in unanticipated performers for your lesser draft choices.

With so few candidates available, goalies are especially important to monitor early on. Raise your hand if you had Carolina Hurricanes waiver pickup Brandon Bussi on your fantasy roster to start 2025-26. Right. After going 31-6-2 (2.44 GAA) in the regular season, the 28-year-old Stanley Cup champion is now considered a top-15 fantasy netminder heading into 2026-27. Your responsibility is to identify this season's Bussi and snag him before anyone else.

One last tip on roster maintenance: Set every day's lineup at the start of the week. You can always shift players around later, but at least there's a reasonable lineup in place if you can't address it for a day or two.

A word on injured reserve

Use those IR slots to your advantage, beginning with the draft. You can always move out such inactive players for others, if necessary, once the league is in full swing. For instance, in all but the shallowest of leagues, Seth Jarvis should be accounted for on draft day, even though he's not expected back from shoulder surgery until November or December. The Carolina forward checks too many fantasy boxes, too well, to leave on the board. The boost he'll provide your squad, once back to health, could prove tangibly beneficial once we're into the meat of the season.

Similarly to the real-life game, it's like trading for a quality player mid-season without giving anything up (other than dumping your biggest roster disappointment). The same applies to Chicago's Connor Bedard, Edmonton's Frederik Andersen, and others. Fill up those IR slots with banged-up placeholders in later stages of your draft. If you need to pivot and jettison Jarvis later because Nathan MacKinnon suffers an injury, so be it.

The art of trades

In my decades of covering and playing fantasy hockey, I've noticed that the most active managers are often the most successful. That goes beyond working the wire. Particularly in deeper leagues, trades are a great way to improve your roster when there's an obvious weakness. Such deals are not tools used to scam another manager. Ideally, both partners come away filling a void. Your goalie for their high-performing winger etc. Maybe you need to address one specific categorical box, such as hits or blocked shots. If most of your fellow managers are trade wary, keep at it. You're likely to find a dance partner eventually. Unless this is you, start with those who are stuck with lousy goaltending. They're usually the most desperate.

With that, here's to a fantastic fantasy season in 2026-27. Good luck!

stories.headline: Pochettino cautious about young stars for USMNT camp amid buzz around Sullivan, Hall
stories.summary: USMNT coach Mauricio Pochettino said that while he is happy about the potential of young players in the U.S. pool, "we need to be careful" amid the buzz around Philadelphia Union's Cavan Sullivan and NYRB's Julian Hall.
stories.body:
United States men's national team coach Mauricio Pochettino said that while he is happy about the potential of young players in the U.S. pool, "we need to be careful" amid the buzz around Philadelphia Union's Cavan Sullivan and Red Bull New York's Julian Hall.

The U.S. has scheduled a quartet of friendlies starting at the end of the month, starting with a match against Peru on Sept. 26, Chile on Sept. 29, Mexico on Oct. 3, and then Canada on Oct. 6. The roster will be announced on Sept. 17, with players beginning to arrive in Atlanta three days later.

As such there is much anticipation about what young players might get called up, including Sullivan and Hall.

Upon signing on for another World Cup cycle last month, Pochettino said he would be "starting from zero" in terms of building his team.

Speaking to reporters via video conference from London, Pochettino stressed he is trying to look at the potential of young players in a balanced way, and not let expectations get ahead of a player's development.

"I think we are very happy about to have all these potential good players being young, and with a possibility to perform and to play," Pochettino said.

"Only we need to be careful. We need to be careful because when you are young, of course you need to be confident, you need to have the trust in yourself, and believe that you can perform and you can do well. But the thing is it's a limit. The balance is the most important.

"And one of our responsibilities is to protect this guy because sometime if you play well and you are 17, 16 or 18 and you play well and people started to know to talk about that you are Messi or you are a big star in the world because you do some few good things. If after you are confused and you don't manage well, that can be dangerous for your career.

"And that is what we don't want. [We want] the young guys with potential being top players to provide the platform for them to evolve and to be professional, to build their career in the best way, improving every day, being humble, being careful when they talk in the media, when they talk with the teammate, when they talk with the opponent. I think respect is the most important thing and they need to be respectful. And of course we want players with talent."

Pochettino said that one goal for this cycle to further eradicate some bad habits that currently exist in the program.

Part of this the alignment of youth and professional clubs with the U.S. Soccer Federation.

The USSF recently announced a takeover of U.S. Youth Soccer.

"I think it's important when we talk about habits, it's about talking about everything, because after the player behave on the field because of this type of decision, they came from the top, he said.

"And we need to be aligned all together in our principles and all the concept that we need to improve if we want to be competitive in every single moment in our [path] until to the first team. I think we are all focused in trying to add our knowledge."

But Pochettino added that the bad habits also include players deciding not to take part competitive tournaments like the Gold Cup.

This a reference to players like Christian Pulisic who opted to sit out the 2025 Gold Cup in order to recover from a long club season.

"We were talking [about] the habit. Before it was difficult to make the roster for the World Cup one year before, because the mindset was different and say, 'Oh, if I play, I have not holidays, I cannot arrive fresh for the World Cup," Pochettino said.

"Already, with the time, you know now that is bulls--- -- sorry -- and I think it's to change this type of idea that are not right and that our experience to build mindset with the coaches, with the people in the organization, in the clubs, and of course us, and then the player that in the way that we will plan and we will do the things is the best for them, for the player, and it's going to be the best for soccer in the USA."

Pochettino added that despite the USMNT playing four games during the window, he will bring in his standard number of 26 players, including four goalkeepers.

Anything more than that would mean some players wouldn't get minutes.

"In this period of the season, we need to be careful with the player that we are going to call," he said.

"We need the players that we'll call that [they] be available to train, but also to play. And I think we consider it at the moment ,and to call 26 players with four keepers. And I think more than this is I think it's an issue because after to train, to share the minutes, I think the player that we are going to have, we want to see, we want to give the possibility to play ... with the possibility to compete. That is the idea for the next camp."

Pochettino indicated that some players who have just switched clubs, like the Middlesbrough duo of defender Max Arfsten and midfielder Sebastian Berhalter, might not be called in in order to give them more time to settle into their new surroundings.

But he indicated there would be a balance between youth and experience.

"I think we cannot bring the whole squad [with] young players because they need to have some guys with experience already competing," Pochettino said.

"But yes, we are going to do a mix ... I think experienced player with young player that can fit together and start to work on how the young kid start to manage the pressure to play in the first team."

stories.body:
Reuben Cotter is free to play in the finals for North Queensland after a former Cowboys under-20s player produced a five-minute clinic as a lawyer at the NRL judiciary.

With Cotter facing the prospect of being rubbed out of Saturday's elimination final against Cronulla, the Cowboys co-captain was initially found guilty of a grade-two high-tackle charge on Tuesday night.

But the lock was able to have the charge reduced to grade-one level with a downgrade bid, resulting in a $1500 fine but freeing him to play in the finals.

Speaking to the panel for just five minutes, Cotter's lawyer Tom Hancock argued his client had only hit Canberra veteran Josh Papalii high because of a bump from North Queensland teammate Coen Hess.

Hancock, who played under-20s for the Cowboys in 2012 and Queensland Cup with Hess, argued his former teammate's involvement in the tackle had resulted in Cotter's body being "bent out of whack".

In turn, Hancock suggested that stopped his client from making a chest-on-chest tackle, and instead sent him upwards and towards Papalii's head.

"He looks set to make contact around the right pec area of Papalii," Hancock told the panel.

"He was entirely rational and what you'd expect of tackling a big dude off a kick off.

"Hess makes contact with Reuben on the outside of his left shoulder. And Reuben's trajectory changes quite drastically from there."

The tackle on Papalii briefly threatened to ruin the Canberra prop's final game in the NRL, before he passed an HIA and scored a try in the Raiders' 50-30 win.

Hancock's argument came after the NRL's legal counsel Lachlan Gyles had claimed Cotter's shoulder had started moving up towards Papalii's head without outside interference.

After initially taking 30 minutes to find Cotter guilty of the high tackle, panel members Henry Perenara and Bob Lindner took just moments to agree to downgrade the charge.

Had the Queensland State of Origin forward lost the case, he would have also missed week two of the finals if North Queensland progress that far.

stories.headline: Despite victory, Real Madrid have a long way to go under Mourinho
stories.summary: Real Madrid were fortunate to defeat Inter Milan, showing how much work remains for Jose Mourinho if they are to win the Champions League.
stories.body:
MADRID -- José Mourinho says he has seen the best and worst of the UEFA Champions League at the Bernabéu. He felt the joy of winning the trophy here in 2010; two years later, he felt the heartbreak of losing a semifinal on penalties.

On Tuesday, in an anxious, awkward 2-1 win over Internazionale, he saw the best and the worst of his new Real Madrid team. If ever a scoreline didn't tell a game's whole story, it was this one.

Inter absolutely dominated the first half, on just about every metric -- take "passes into the attacking third": Madrid 15, Inter 128 -- except the bottom line.

Madrid were 2-0 up after 23 minutes, Kylian Mbappé and Federico Valverde taking quick-thinking advantage of Inter's defensive mistakes, and they could have scored again before halftime.

But the balance of play was completely in Inter's favor. In the second half, Madrid improved and could have scored three more goals, although it was Inter who found the net through Carlos Augusto in the 77th minute to ensure a tense finale.

Mourinho might not have minded. "I want to win," he'd said on Monday in his prematch news conference. "I could say I want to play well, but I don't want to play well like we did against [Real] Betis [in LaLiga on Friday] and lose. I want to win."

He got his wish. Madrid won, starting Mourinho's quest to win a trophy that eluded him during his previous three seasons at the Bernabéu -- falling each time at the semifinal stage between 2010 and 2013 -- with three points in the league phase.

But radical, across-the-board improvement will be needed for this Madrid team to be considered contenders to make it all the way to the final at the neighboring Metropolitano Stadium in June.

Some context: This was a Madrid team without the suspended Arda Güler, who has arguably been their best player so far this season. His only contribution on Tuesday was to collect last season's Champions League Breakthrough Player Award before kickoff. There was also no Bernardo Silva, the player who has been earmarked to give Madrid a degree of midfield control that they lacked in 2025-26.

In their place was Trent Alexander-Arnold, playing out of position in central midfield and looking lost, unsure of where to be and what to do.

Madrid still have outstanding players capable of deciding games with their individual talent. In goal, Thibaut Courtois made seven saves. Just one of Inter's 17 chances -- four of them defined by Opta as "big chances" -- was converted, by Augusto.

And at the other end of the pitch, there is Mbappé, scorer of 15 Champions League goals last season. Prematch, he had bristled at suggestions he ought to work harder and be more of a hard-working, modern forward like PSG's Ousmane Dembélé or Barcelona's Raphinha.

"I could say I score more goals than the two players you mentioned," he responded. "But I want to be smart and say of course I need to improve ... even if I do things those others don't."

Four days before the Inter game, at Real Betis, Mbappé had a rare off night, with seven shots and a personal expected-goals (xG) total of 1.96 -- including a missed penalty -- going unrewarded.

Here he put Madrid ahead after 14 minutes, after a move Dembélé or Raphinha would have been proud of. Spotting that Inter midfielder Curtis Jones' pass had put teammate Yann Bisseck under pressure, Mbappé closed Bisseck down and forced him into a panicked mistake, with Brahim Díaz providing the pass for Mbappé to finish.

An even more glaring error put Madrid 2-0 up, with Valverde closing down Inter goalkeeper Josep Martínez. Valverde was later named the game's MVP but said it should have been Courtois. "He saved us," he told Movistar.

Before halftime, both Mbappé and Jude Bellingham could have made it 3-0. Bellingham went close again after the break. But there was always something deeply unconvincing about Madrid's performance, a lack of control, and an inability to impose themselves on the game. Inter were more assured, and more composed.

Madrid fans who should have been feeling buoyant about a lead against another top European team were instead frustrated. Some of them whistled Vinícius Júnior when he was substituted in the 87th minute, and a few even whistled Mbappé when he was withdrawn in added time.

Inter ended the match with more possession, more shots and more of the ball in dangerous areas, even if the clearest chances had been Madrid's.

Mourinho has denied he's lacking a Champions League with Madrid, that he must win it because he was unable to do in his first spell. "We won what we won, and we lost what we lost," he said prematch about what's missing from his personal Bernabéu trophy cabinet. "It's a closed chapter."

It's early -- just five competitive games played, one of them in Europe -- but to write a new one, with the ending he wants, Mourinho must find this team's new identity, one that isn't overreliant on Courtois at one end, and Mbappé at the other.

stories.headline: Pelicans trade Jordan Hawkins to Grizzlies in 4-player deal
stories.summary: The Pelicans have traded Jordan Hawkins, Micah Peavy, a future second-round draft pick and a future second-round pick swap to the Grizzlies for AJ Johnson and Taj Gibson.
stories.body:
The New Orleans Pelicans have traded Jordan Hawkins, Micah Peavy, a future second-round draft pick and a future second-round pick swap to the Memphis Grizzlies for AJ Johnson and Taj Gibson.

The trade, which was announced Tuesday, clears roster space for the Pelicans, frees up salary flexibility to sign Bennedict Mathurin to a two-year, $16 million deal, and allows New Orleans to have a look at a young player in the 21-year-old Johnson, who was the No. 21 pick in the 2024 draft.

Hawkins, a lottery pick at No. 14 in the 2023 draft, now gets dealt by his team prior to his fourth season.

The Grizzlies, who picked up draft assets in the deal, will have multiple roster decisions before the start of the season as they are several guaranteed contracts above the 15 maximum.

Hawkins, 24, averaged 5.1 points in 51 games last season and struggled to find consistent playing time in New Orleans' crowded backcourt rotation. The former UConn star played just 13.6 minutes per game, a significant decrease from the 2024-25 season, when he played 23.6 minutes per game and averaged 10.8 points per game.

The Pelicans will be the fifth team in three seasons for the 6-foot-5 Johnson, who split last season between the Washington Wizards and Dallas Mavericks.

The Mavericks traded Johnson to the Grizzlies for Santi Aldama in July, five months after Johnson was included in the Anthony Davis blockbuster trade between Dallas and Washington. Johnson was drafted by the Milwaukee Bucks in 2024 before being traded later that season to the Wizards.

The trade saves New Orleans $5.7 million in salary, according to ESPN's Bobby Marks. Johnson was not allowed to be aggregated in a deal until Tuesday -- two months from the Aldama trade.

Gibson, 41, appeared in 10 games with Memphis last season. The 17-year veteran has played for eight different teams in his NBA career.

The 6-foot-7 Peavy appeared in 61 games as a rookie last season for the Pelicans, averaging 4.3 points.
